The Cantor Function

This scene climbs the Cantor function, the Devil's staircase. It is continuous and always rising, yet flat on almost every interval.

The function pauses on every gap of the Cantor set. So its slope is zero at almost every point. And still it climbs from 0 to 1 overall. The total climb disagrees with the sum of slopes.

For example, climb a 🪜 staircase whose landings are endlessly long. You rest almost the whole way, yet you still reach the top. The Cantor function does exactly that.

Show proof

  1. The complement of the Cantor set is the disjoint union of the removed open middle thirds.

    Each interval removed at stage mmm has the form (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) with a=0.c1…cm−113a = 0.c_1\ldots c_{m-1}1_3a=0.c1​…cm−1​13​ (terminating) and b=0.c1…cm−123b = 0.c_1\ldots c_{m-1}2_3b=0.c1​…cm−1​23​, where c1,…,cm−1c_1,\ldots,c_{m-1}c1​,…,cm−1​ contain no 111.

Compute that f(1)−f(0)=1f(1) - f(0) = 1f(1)−f(0)=1 yet ∫01f′=0\int_0^1 f' = 0∫01​f′=0, and prove that fff is therefore not absolutely continuous.

This is why the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus needs a stronger hypothesis than "differentiable almost everywhere".

(The definition of absolute continuity itself may be stated at idea level.)

Show proof

  1. By problem 1, fff is continuous on [0,1][0,1][0,1] with f(0)=0f(0) = 0f(0)=0 and f(1)=1f(1) = 1f(1)=1, so f(1)−f(0)=1f(1) - f(0) = 1f(1)−f(0)=1.

    On the other hand, problem 2 gives only that f′=0f' = 0f′=0 on the complement of the Cantor set.

    But that complement has length 111 and the Cantor set CCC has measure 000, so f′=0f' = 0f′=0 a.e. (the values on CCC do not affect an a.e. statement).

    Combined with Lebesgue's theorem that a monotone function is differentiable almost everywhere, the (Lebesgue) integral is ∫01f′=0\int_0^1 f' = 0∫01​f′=0.

    An absolutely continuous function with f′=0f' = 0f′=0 a.e. must be constant, which is the heart of the contradiction below.

  2. If fff were absolutely continuous, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus would give f(1)−f(0)=∫01f′f(1) - f(0) = \int_0^1 f'f(1)−f(0)=∫01​f′.

    But 1≠01 \neq 01=0 — a contradiction.

    Hence fff is not absolutely continuous: continuity plus differentiability almost everywhere does not imply the FTC.

    "Differentiable almost everywhere" is not enough to recover a function by integration; absolute continuity is the sharp hypothesis.

  3. This can also be seen directly.

    Absolute continuity means: for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that any finite family of disjoint intervals with total length below δ\deltaδ has total ∣f∣|f|∣f∣-increment below ε\varepsilonε.

    Take ε=1/2\varepsilon = 1/2ε=1/2.

    The 2n2^n2n intervals of CnC_nCn​ have total length (2/3)n→0(2/3)^n \to 0(2/3)n→0, eventually below any δ\deltaδ.

    But fff is constant on the gaps between them and nondecreasing, so ∑i(f(ri)−f(li))=f(1)−f(0)=1≥ε\sum_i (f(r_i) - f(l_i)) = f(1) - f(0) = 1 \ge \varepsilon∑i​(f(ri​)−f(li​))=f(1)−f(0)=1≥ε — every δ\deltaδ fails.

    The Cantor set is nearly 000 in length yet covers all of [0,1][0,1][0,1] in fff-value (fff maps CCC onto [0,1][0,1][0,1]).
